shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example overlaying the wrong version at values a child suggests and measuring the gap.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

title_framing.normal: Free Play · Square Of Sum Tiles

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to put the whole four-tile structure on screen at once, because the misconception is a MISSING PIECE and a student cannot miss what they have never seen. Both edges are cut at the same mark and the cut is drawn travelling, so the class sees the square forcing the two cuts to agree — that is the whole reason there are two rectangles and not one.

Beat 2 is the argument for the 2, and it is a counting argument rather than a rule. The two rectangle tiles are lit together; they report the SAME area and they sit on OPPOSITE corners. Read the four-term line out loud before the collapsed one — 9 plus 12 plus 12 plus 16 — because collapsing straight to 2ab is exactly where the doubling stops being visible.

Beat 3 turns the refutation into a measurement. The overlay is drawn to true scale, so at 3 plus 4 it covers 25 of 49 and the uncovered band is over half the picture. Say the shortfall as a number the tool computed — two times three times four is twenty-four square units — and never as you forgot the middle term.

media.title: The missing middle in a square of a sum
media.context: This hook opens the topic on the square of a sum and of a difference. Students know how a product grows. The film must not give the middle term, must not give the correct square and must not state the identity.
media.description: Somebody squares fifty three as two thousand five hundred plus nine and gets it wrong, because a real piece of area has quietly vanished. Where does the middle term hide when a square is split, and why is it so easy to drop?
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Expand the square of a sum and of a difference, and account for the middle term. Key teaching points: 1) A square split into two parts gives four regions, not two. 2) Two of them are the squares of the parts. 3) The other two are identical strips, giving twice the product. 4) The square of a difference has the same middle term with a minus sign. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often square each part and add, dropping the middle term. 2) Students often forget that the two strips are equal in area. Pause points: 0:21, at the end of a vanished strip: ask what fifty three squared should really be. 0:21, just before the open question: ask how many regions the split square has. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what the two missing strips are worth. After viewing, ask why there are two of them and not one.

content.text: Squaring a sum is not the same as squaring each part. Draw a square whose side is a + b. Splitting it gives four regions: an a by a corner of area a squared, a b by b corner of area b squared, and two a by b rectangles. The two rectangles together have area 2ab, so (a + b) squared = a squared + 2ab + b squared. The 2ab is real area sitting in the middle, which is exactly the piece dropped by anyone who writes only a squared + b squared. Splitting a number like 53 into 50 + 3 turns a hard square into three easy pieces.

content.text: To square a difference, start from a big square of side a with area a squared and shrink it to side a - b. You remove two strips of width b, each of area ab, which subtracts 2ab. But those two strips overlap at the small b by b corner, so that corner has been removed twice. Adding it back once gives (a - b) squared = a squared - 2ab + b squared. The middle term is subtracted, yet the last term is always positive, because it is a restored corner. Splitting a number like 97 into 100 - 3 makes its square easy.

topics.publication_chunk: Squaring a sum is not the same as squaring each part. Draw a square whose side is a + b. Splitting it gives four regions: an a by a corner of area a squared, a b by b corner of area b squared, and two a by b rectangles. The two rectangles together have area 2ab, so (a + b) squared = a squared + 2ab + b squared. The 2ab is real area sitting in the middle, which is exactly the piece dropped by anyone who writes only a squared + b squared. Splitting a number like 53 into 50 + 3 turns a hard square into three easy pieces. Worked examples of a square of a sum has a middle, demonstrated one step at a time across different cases. Splitting it gives four regions: an a by a corner of area a squared, a b by b corner of area b squared, and two a by b rectangles. The two rectangles together have area 2ab, so (a + b) squared = a squared + 2ab + b squared. The 2ab is real area sitting in the middle, which is exactly the piece dropped by anyone who writes only a squared + b squared. Splitting a number like 53 into 50 + 3 turns a hard square into three easy pieces. To square a difference, start from a big square of side a with area a squared and shrink it to side a - b. You remove two strips of width b, each of area ab, which subtracts 2ab. But those two strips overlap at the small b by b corner, so that corner has been removed twice. Adding it back once gives (a - b) squared = a squared - 2ab + b squared. The middle term is subtracted, yet the last term is always positive, because it is a restored corner. content.text: Take a square of side a and cut a smaller square of side b from one corner. What is left is an L-shape of area a squared minus b squared. Cut the L-shape into two pieces and slide them together, and they form one rectangle whose sides are a + b and a - b. So a squared minus b squared = (a + b)(a - b). You can also see it in algebra: (a + b)(a - b) = a squared - ab + ab - b squared, and the two middle terms cancel. This makes products like 47 times 53 easy, since they are (50 - 3)(50 + 3) = 2500 - 9.

topics.summary: Two numbers either side of a round centre multiply to the centre squared minus the gap squared, and a square is a round product plus a small square, so products like 96 x 104 and squares like 96 squared are found in one line.

content.text: The identities turn awkward products into easy ones. If two numbers sit the same distance d either side of a round centre c, then their product is (c - d)(c + d) = c squared minus d squared. For example 96 times 104 is 100 squared minus 4 squared = 9984. To square a number a, use a squared = (a + d)(a - d) + d squared, which is a round product plus a small square, so 96 squared = 100 times 92 + 16 = 9216. The correction is always the gap squared, never just the gap.

media.title: Catching the dropped middle term
media.context: The commonest algebra mistake is writing the square of a sum as the sum of the squares, which drops the middle term. The worked example examines a student writing the bracket x plus 5 squared as x squared plus 25 and asks whether it is correct. The figure expands fully and shows what is missing.
media.description: Catching the dropped middle term: a labelled figure illustrating the idea, drawn from the worked example 'A student writes (x + 5) squared = x squared + 25. Correct or not? If not, mend it'.

source_image.alt: Diagram for catching the dropped middle term.
source_image.caption: Catching the dropped middle term: a labelled figure illustrating the idea, drawn from the worked example 'A student writes (x + 5) squared = x squared + 25. Correct or not? If not, mend it'.

media.teaching_notes: Substitute a number into both forms first; the numerical gap makes the error undeniable. Then find the gap on the picture. Ask what the middle term is in general.
media.negative_prompt: photorealistic rendering, photographic texture, 3D modelling, isometric or perspective projection, drop shadows, gradients, glossy or metallic surfaces, neon glow; decorative clutter, background scenery, ornamental borders, frames, mascots, emoji, speech bubbles that carry no information; watermarks, signatures, logos, stock imagery, colour swatches; garbled or misspelled words, invented digits, duplicated or contradictory labels, handwriting and script fonts, wording in any script other than English; text cropped at the edge, labels overlapping the figure, type too small to read at half size; any wording at all beyond the listed labels, including added titles, captions, summaries, or a sentence describing what the figure shows; the claim shown without a cross; a check whose arithmetic is wrong; a middle term other than 10x; the two rectangles drawn at different sizes; a correction that changes anything other than the middle term
media.generation_prompt: Flat educational vector illustration in the style of an NCERT Grade 8 mathematics textbook: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines, a restrained palette of one teal accent, one amber accent and neutral grey, flat fills with no shading and no gradients, all wording in a clean sans-serif, 16:9 landscape at 1456 by 816 pixels. Scene: The student's claim is written at the top as a card reading (x + 5) squared = x squared + 25, with a bold cross beside it. Below, a split square of side x plus 5 is drawn with its four regions labelled x squared, 5x, 5x and 25, with the two 5x rectangles tinted amber and ringed as the missing part. A correct expansion strip reads 'x squared + 10x + 25', with the middle term ringed and a tag reading the dropped middle term is 2ab. A numerical check panel substitutes x equal to 4 into both forms, giving 81 for the correct expansion and 41 for the claim, with a difference tag reading 40, which matches 2 times 4 times 5. Draw no wording at all except the following, which is the complete and only text in the figure, spelled exactly like this: (x + 5) squared = x squared + 25; x squared; 5x; 5x; 25; the missing middle term; x squared + 10x + 25; at x = 4: 81 and 41; the difference is 40, which is 2ab.
media.accuracy_constraints:
The student's claim must be clearly crossed.
The correct expansion must be x squared plus 10x plus 25.
The two middle rectangles must be identical and identified as the missing term.
The numerical check at x equal to 4 must give 81 and 41, differing by 40.
The difference must be shown to equal 2 times 4 times 5.
Every number, count and label drawn in the figure must match this brief exactly; no value may be invented, rounded or added.
Use NCERT Ganita Prakash Grade 8 wording for every term, keep British spelling, and write no sentence that a Grade 8 reader could not read aloud.

media.title: Spotting the slip that flips a sign
media.context: This hook opens the topic on catching common mistakes. Students know the identities. The film must not name either slip and must not correct anything.
media.description: A bracket is opened, one sign comes out wrong, and the whole answer breaks. Some mistakes repeat again and again, and the same two slips spoil most simplifications.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Find and name the common slips in expanding brackets and simplifying. Key teaching points: 1) The middle term is the piece most often dropped. 2) A minus outside a bracket must reach every term inside. 3) Unlike terms cannot be combined, however tempting. 4) Naming the cause of a slip makes the correction obvious. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often write the square of a difference as a difference of squares. 2) Students often combine unlike terms when tidying an answer. Pause points: 0:23, at the end of the same two slips: ask what is wrong with the line on screen. 0:23, just before the open question: ask which slip the class makes most often. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what the square of a difference really expands to. After viewing, ask what a minus outside a bracket must reach.

topics.summary: Each claimed simplification is judged correct or incorrect and then mended: squares keep a middle 2ab, a negative multiplier flips every sign, and only like terms combine.

content.text: The most common algebra mistake is writing (a + b) squared as a squared + b squared. This drops the middle term 2ab, the two equal rectangles in the split square. To judge any squaring claim, expand it fully: (a + b) squared = a squared + 2ab + b squared. If the claim has no middle term, it is wrong, and the fix is to put back twice the product of the parts. A claim is only correct when its middle term is already there, so not every square is wrong. Naming the cause, the forgotten rectangles, is what makes the fix obvious.

content.text: Common mistakes in algebraic simplification can be identified and corrected by carefully checking the rules being applied. When a negative multiplier is distributed across a bracket, it must affect every term and change the sign of each term it reaches. Also, only like terms—terms having exactly the same variables with the same powers—can be combined. For example, terms such as 7w² and 4w cannot be combined because their powers are different. By observing each step and identifying the reason for an incorrect simplification, the correct method becomes clear.
content.publication_text: Two slips spoil most simplifications. First, a negative multiplier must reach every term in the bracket and flips each sign, and a negative times a negative gives a positive, so -6(2m - 5) = -12m + 30. Second, only like terms combine, meaning terms with exactly the same letters and powers, so 7w squared + 4w stays as it is and a squared b never joins with ab squared. To judge a claim, distribute carefully with the sign rules, then collect only the truly like terms. A mistake always has a named cause, and the fix follows from naming it.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer why writing a square of a sum term by term gives a wrong answer through observation and reasoning, and determine that the quantity a plus b squared is a squared plus 2ab plus b squared and never a squared plus b squared for non-zero parts. They will explain that the dropped 2ab is the two equal rectangles of the split square, so a claim missing its middle term is wrong and the fix restores twice the product of the parts.

learning_objectives.strand_name: Catching errors and seeing many methods as one
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to observe and identify common mistakes made during algebraic simplification, explain why a particular step is incorrect, and determine the appropriate correction using sign rules and the rules for combining like terms. They will recognize that a negative multiplier affects every term inside a bracket and that only terms with the same letters and powers can be combined.

media.title: Identity Generaliser
media.context: CBSE Class 8, NCERT Ganita Prakash Chapter 6 'We Distribute, Yet Things Multiply', the Generalise beat. Every identity in this chapter has been built from an area picture; this is where the student has to say what the picture claims in general and defend what the letters are allowed to be. The worked claim is the square of a sum, and the rule it is set against is the class's own over-generalisation of distributivity, (a + b)squared = a squared + b squared, which agrees exactly when a is 0 or b is 0.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's statement, the canonical identity, and the test that settled it.
whatYouLearned: A general statement is a claim about every pair of numbers, not about the cases checked
One failing substitution ends a statement, however many cases agreed
Negative and fractional values are the fastest way to test a claimed rule

overview.goal: The student converts a set of verified numeric cases into a general statement with letters and defends what the letters are allowed to be.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A working page with the checked cases listed down one side, a large statement box on the other, and a results table beneath both. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: Four cases in a row have worked, and the class is asked whether that settles anything.
overview.concept: Several numeric cases that agree suggest a rule but do not establish it. Writing the rule with letters makes it a claim about every pair of numbers, and it can then be tested at values the cases never covered, including negatives and fractions. A statement that survives awkward values is worth trusting; one that fails at a single value is finished.
overview.purpose: The student converts a set of verified numeric cases into a general statement with letters and defends what the letters are allowed to be.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Cases left and statement box right on a wide frame, cases above the box on a 390 px frame. The test table sits beneath at both widths and scrolls vertically rather than shrinking. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not show any general form while a prediction is still open, and never rewrite what the student typed. A repaired statement would test something the student did not claim.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. A general statement is a claim about every substitution, so testing it at values chosen to be awkward is the fastest way to find out whether it is really general. Negative and fractional values matter because a rule read off whole number cases often quietly assumes them. Surviving those does not prove the statement, but failing any one of them ends it immediately. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): A case chosen where the disputed term vanishes tests nothing. Breaks: Believing any case that works is evidence for a rule. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): The wrong rule holds on a thin set of cases, which is why checking a few can mislead. Breaks: Treating agreement in some cases as agreement in general. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): Letters are what turn a pattern into a statement about every number. Breaks: The empirical proof scheme, treating checked cases as a proof. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): A counterexample can be tiny, so failing to find one is not evidence. Breaks: Believing a rule that survives easy cases will survive the rest. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): A general statement is a different kind of object from a list of verified cases. Breaks: Reading the letters as standing for particular numbers rather than for any number.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with four numeric cases that all worked and asks the class to write the rule they think holds for every pair. Beat 2 takes the committed statement and tests it at fresh values, including a negative and a fraction. Beat 3 reports the first failing case, or promotes a surviving statement to the chapter's identity card with the class's name on it. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with addCase, testStatement, promoteIdentity and say.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open with four verified numeric cases listed, the statement box empty and the results table empty, and ask the class for the rule they think holds for every pair of numbers. Commit the class statement on the prediction pad. Target the four listed cases. Never test a value before the statement is committed. Call 2. Run the committed statement at fresh values, including one negative and one fraction, and let each result land in the table. Targets the test table and the sample controls. Read both sides of each row from getState().truth. Call 3. Give the verdict from the table, naming the first disagreeing row or promoting the statement to the identity card. Targets the failing row and the identity card. Never call a statement proved because it survived; say what it survived.

observationsAndConclusions.why: Cases are instances, while a statement is a claim about all of them at once
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Four agreeing cases sit beside a statement that still fails at the fifth value
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Agreement on examples is evidence for a statement and never a proof of it

observationsAndConclusions.why: The letters are placeholders, so renaming them changes nothing about the claim

observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A general statement is about structure, not about which letters were used to write it

media.description: A claim about every pair of numbers stands in a card on the right, typeset the way the chapter types it, with a test table beneath holding one row per substitution and an area square on the left showing the same claim as a picture. The square is a square of side a + b cut into its four regions by ONE scale function, so the two identical ab rectangles are drawn to scale and, when the claim on the card leaves them out, they are drawn hollow with the exact gap the two sides differ by printed underneath. Every row of the table is produced by parsing the claim into an expression tree and evaluating both sides in exact rational arithmetic, so 1/2 and 1/3 are compared as fractions rather than as decimals and no correct statement is ever marked wrong by a floating point comparison. The sample set always carries a pair whose product is zero, tagged 2ab = 0 so an agreeing row is visibly worth nothing, a negative pair and a fractional pair. Rows land one at a time and the first disagreeing row holds and stops the rest, which makes a counterexample the end of an argument rather than one row among many. A statement that survives every row is offered for promotion to the chapter identity card, worded survived rather than proved.

concept.notation: A general statement uses letters that stand for any number, not for a particular one and not for an object. The tester substitutes values for those letters.
concept.statement: Several numeric cases that agree suggest a rule but do not establish it. Writing the rule with letters makes it a claim about every pair of numbers, and it can then be tested at values the cases never covered, including negatives and fractions. A statement that survives awkward values is worth trusting; one that fails at a single value is finished.
prerequisites: the identities built in this chapter
substituting a value for a letter
misconceptions: The letters read as specific numbers, so the rule is thought to be about the cases that were checked.
The letters read as labels for objects rather than as any number.
concept.why_it_is_true: A general statement is a claim about every substitution, so testing it at values chosen to be awkward is the fastest way to find out whether it is really general. Negative and fractional values matter because a rule read off whole number cases often quietly assumes them. Surviving those does not prove the statement, but failing any one of them ends it immediately.
worked_numbers: Cases at 3 and 4, 5 and 2, 6 and 1 all fit the square of a sum, and the general form is a squared plus 2ab plus b squared.
Testing at a equal to minus 3 and b equal to 2 keeps working, which a rule assuming positives might not.
Testing at a equal to one half catches a statement that only holds for whole numbers.

addTestValueOutcomes.zero: a row where several terms vanish, so a wrong statement can pass it by accident
addTestValueOutcomes.fraction: a row that breaks any statement quietly assuming its letters are whole numbers
addTestValueOutcomes.negative: a row that breaks any statement quietly assuming its letters are positive
addTestValueOutcomes.wholePositive: an ordinary row that most statements survive, so it decides very little

testStatementOutcomes.failed: the first disagreeing row is named and held in the warning tone
testStatementOutcomes.survived: every sample row agrees on both sides and the statement is offered for promotion
testStatementOutcomes.unreadable: the statement could not be parsed, and the tool says what it could not read rather than marking it wrong

promoteIdentityOutcomes.refused: promotion is refused while any sample row disagrees, and the failing row is shown
promoteIdentityOutcomes.accepted: the statement is written onto the chapter identity card in the student's own words

answer_key.worked: The general statement must hold for every substitution, including negatives and fractions, and one failing value ends it.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the typed statement: its value on both sides at many sample points, and the first sample where they disagree.
answer_key.precision: The typed statement is parsed into an expression tree and both sides are evaluated at many sample points including negative and fractional values. Nothing is ever accepted on a string match.
answer_key.ground_truth: canonicalIdentity = the target identity, held per item. holdsAt(statement, values) = both sides evaluate equal at that substitution. firstFailure(statement) = the first sample point where they disagree, reported as a counterexample.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.case: A statement that holds for whole numbers only
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Caught by the fractional test values, and the first failing sample is reported as a counterexample rather than as a mark.

edge_cases.case: A statement written with different letters
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Accepted, because the tester substitutes into whatever letters were used. Only the structure matters, not the choice of symbol.

edge_cases.case: A statement that is true but not the target identity
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: It survives testing and the tool says so, noting that it is a different true statement. Surviving is about truth, not about matching an expected answer.

edge_cases.case: A student supplied test value

hostProps.questions: TOP LEVEL. The Practice bank the platform drew for this concept, from question_bank_v2 where delivery_mode = 'Practice'. Read it as props.questions ?? props.additionalProps?.questions, top level first. When it is non empty it REPLACES the authored practice bank.

hostProps.enabledModes: Which of the four modes exist this session.
hostProps.learnQuestions: TOP LEVEL. The Learn bank for this concept, from question_bank_v2 where delivery_mode = 'Learn', mandatory checkpoints first. Read it as props.learnQuestions ?? props.additionalProps?.learnQuestions. When it is non empty those items ARE the Learn steps; the authored scene examples are only the fallback for a thin pool.
hostProps.showModeSelector: false in production for every maths tool. Honour it, defaulting to true (const showSelector = props.showModeSelector ?? true) so the selector still works in preview and review, and disappears live.
hostProps.additionalProps.exampleSeed: A 32 bit int the tool's mulberry32 PRNG consumes directly. The teacher agent builds its own copy of the example set from the SAME seed, so Math.random(), Date.now() or ignoring the seed desynchronises the narration from the screen in every single session.

caseSet.description: The verified numeric cases shown before the student generalises.

questions.description: Replaces the built in practice bank. Items are {kind:'generalise', cases:object[], target:string} | {kind:'add_test', statement:string} | {kind:'letter_scope'} | {kind:'choice', prompt, options[], correct, explain}.

testValues.description: The sample points the tester uses, which always include at least one negative and one fractional value.

constraints: The tester uses the student's statement verbatim and never repairs it, so what is tested is what was written.
The statement is parsed into an expression tree and both sides are evaluated at many sample points; nothing is accepted on a string match.
The sample set always includes negative and fractional values, because a rule read off whole number cases often assumes them silently.
The first failing sample is reported as a counterexample rather than as a mark, so the student learns what killed the statement.
A surviving statement is promoted to the chapter identity card with the student's name, so a generalisation is treated as an achievement rather than a step.

extra.concept_only: Concept carries no questions of its own. Its beats reveal the idea and then run one reasoning beat each, and every number the agent says is read from state.truth.

ai.shows: The verified cases, the general statement box, the test results table, the teacher caption, and discrete step navigation (Prev / Step k of 3 / Next) with a progress bar.
steps: Predict: four numeric cases are listed, all of which worked, and the statement box is empty. The class commits the rule they think holds for every pair, out loud, and the teacher commits it on the pad. prediction_made unlocks the beat.
Test: the committed statement is run at fresh values, including a negative and a fraction, and each result lands in the table.
Verdict: the first failing case is named, or the statement is promoted to the chapter identity card.
ai.done_when: Beat 3 has been reached and the statement has either failed at a named value or been promoted. Concept has no Finish button.
ai.driven_by: The teaching agent, through next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) and the component calls.
ai.opens_with: Four verified numeric cases listed with an empty general statement box and an empty test table, the predict pad open on 'These four numeric cases all worked. Write the rule you think holds for every pair of numbers.'.

normal.shows: The cases, the statement box, the test table, every control, no score and no question.
steps: No steps. Nothing is mandatory and nothing is scored.
normal.done_when: The student presses Finish, which emits finished once.
normal.opens_with: An empty case list with the statement box and test controls live.
play_modes: SWITCH IT OFF: find a pair where the middle term is 0 and say why that pair cannot test the rule.
SMALLEST BREAK: find the smallest pair of counting numbers that breaks the wrong rule.
CASE TO LETTER: check three pairs of your own, then write the statement the three cases point at.
REGION HUNT: name which region of the area picture each term of the statement counts.
normal.parameter_freedom: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example testing a statement a child offers at a value designed to break it.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to make the wrong rule TEMPTING before it is broken. All four listed cases really do agree, because each of them switches the middle term off, and the class has to be allowed to feel that four agreeing cases look like evidence. Never open beat 2 before the class has said out loud what they think the four cases settle.

Beat 2 is the whole argument in one move: one pair the four cases never covered ends the claim, and the square redrawn at a = 1, b = 1 shows exactly what was left out — two of the four equal quarters, the gap of 2. Point at the two hollow quarters and let the class read 4 against 2 off the row.

Beat 3 turns the same instrument on the true identity and adds the letter-scope move: the identical rows appear again with the claim written in p and q, so the letters visibly carry no number of their own. media.title: Three different expressions, one and the same number
media.context: This hook opens the topic on different pictures giving one number. Students know the identities. The film must not expand any formula and must not say why they agree.
media.description: Three classmates count the same growing pattern and write three formulas that look nothing alike, and yet all three always agree. How can such different expressions give one number at every step?
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: See that different correct descriptions of one pattern must be equal expressions. Key teaching points: 1) A pattern can be counted in several honest ways. 2) Each way gives a different looking formula. 3) All of them count the same objects, so they must agree. 4) Expanding each to a common form proves it. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often think only one formula can be correct. 2) Students often check agreement on one case and stop. Pause points: 0:23, at the end of they never disagree: ask how the class would count the pattern. 0:23, just before the open question: ask what would settle the argument for good. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask whether two different formulas can both be right. After viewing, ask how to prove two expressions equal.

topics.summary: A circle pattern counted several ways gives expressions like (k + 1) squared minus 1, k(k + 2) and k squared + 2k, all of which expand to k squared + 2k and so agree at every step.

content.text: A growing pattern can be counted in many ways, and the expressions look different: (k + 1) squared minus 1, k times (k + 2), and k times (k + 1) plus k all describe the same circles. Each one expands to k squared + 2k, so they are equal for every step k, not just the ones drawn. This is the point of algebra: it proves that different pictures give one number for all k at once. Checking a few steps can only suggest a pattern; expanding to a common form proves it.

media.context: CBSE Class 8, NCERT Ganita Prakash Ch.6 'We Distribute, Yet Things Multiply', closing the chapter's structural thread. Every identity has been met as an EXPANSION — the chapter never uses the word factorise — so the bins carry the written forms and the tool says 'can be written as a product', never 'factorises'. It is read after all three identities are known, where the student has to decide which one an expression is asking for, and it rehearses the 1-mark board reading and the 2-mark 'which number is squared' item directly.

finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's placement, the correct bin, and the structural note that explains it.
whatYouLearned: An identity is chosen by reading a structure, not by spotting a squared term
A difference of two squares factorises and a sum of two squares does not
Some expressions match none of the identities, and saying so is a correct answer

overview.goal: The student matches an expression to the identity that fits its structure, and writes what feature triggered each choice.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A sorting table with four labelled bins in a row and a spread of expression cards lying face up beneath them. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A card that looks factorisable turns out not to be, and the class is asked which feature decides.
overview.concept: Choosing an identity is reading a structure. A difference of two squares has a minus between two squares; a sum of two squares has a plus and does not factorise at all. A squared bracket signals a square of a sum or difference according to its inner sign. Some expressions fit none of them, which is why the none bin always has members.
overview.purpose: The student matches an expression to the identity that fits its structure, and writes what feature triggered each choice.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Bins across the upper main panel, card table beneath. On a 390 px frame the bins wrap to two rows and the table scrolls horizontally. Every card keeps a 44 px hit target. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not pre-place any card while a prediction is still open, and never let the none bin be empty. An empty none bin would let the sort be finished by elimination.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. The identities are statements about particular shapes, so an expression only matches when its shape agrees. The sign between the two squares is the whole difference between a factorisable expression and one that is not, which is why a near miss card is a genuine test rather than a trick. Keeping the none bin non empty stops the sort from being solvable by elimination. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): The minus sign is the feature that triggers the identity, not the two squares. Breaks: A sum of two squares treated as factorisable by analogy with the difference. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): A perfect square trinomial is recognised by the middle term matching twice the product. Breaks: Matching an identity by the number of terms alone rather than by structure. ML3 (Medium, Edge Case): The sign of the middle term chooses between the two square identities; the last term stays positive in both. Breaks: Expecting a minus in the middle to leave a minus in the last term. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): The identity needs BOTH terms to be squares, not just the minus sign. Breaks: Triggering the identity on the minus sign alone. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): Identities are selected by structure, not by surface resemblance. Breaks: Choosing an identity because the expression looks like a remembered example.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the whole card set and the bins EMPTY, and asks which bin will get the fewest cards. Beat 2 sorts the clean cases, each card landing by its structure rather than by its look. Beat 3 introduces a sum of two squares, which cannot be factorised and belongs in the none bin, so the bins are shown not to cover everything. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with placeCard, expandCard, revealBin and say. No drag: the agent places a card by naming its bin.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open with the whole card spread face up and all four bins empty, and ask the class which bin will end up with the fewest cards. Commit the class bin on the prediction pad. Target the card table. Never place a card before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Place the clean cases one at a time and ask for the feature that decided each, holding the class on the sign and the middle term. Targets the three identity bins and the bin counts. Read each card's expansion from getState().truth. Call 3. Offer a sum of two squares and let it go to the none bin, then ask what would have to change for it to move. Targets the none bin and the expanded card. Never leave the none bin empty at the end of the sort.

hunts: SUM TRAP: find three expressions that look factorisable but are sums of two squares.

media.description: Four bins stand in a row, each labelled with a written form first and its plain name second — (a + b)², (a − b)², (a + b)(a − b), and a fourth for none of these — with the structural test that admits a card printed underneath. Expression cards lie on a table beneath them. A card is sorted by reading its structure: how many terms it has, whether the outer terms are whole squares, and what sign joins them. Opening a card draws the NCERT region picture for it, and that picture is what settles every claim rather than a caption: (x + 3)² is a square cut into x², two identical 3x strips and a 3 × 3 corner; x² − 9 is a square with a 3 × 3 corner cut out, re-cut beside it as an (x + 3) by (x − 3) rectangle of exactly equal area; x² + 9 is drawn as two separate squares beside the square (x + 3)(x + 3) would have needed, whose two strips have nothing on the card to match; x² + 5x + 9 puts the 6x the strips make against the 5x the card carries, one x short on the same scale; and x² − 5 is drawn as 4, then 5, then 9, so 5 visibly has no square. A card placed in the wrong bin comes back to the table carrying the feature that decided it, so the reason arrives with the card rather than as a mark. The set always holds at least one card that fits no identity, so the none bin is never empty and the sort can never be finished by elimination.

Beat 3 introduces a sum of two squares, which cannot be factorised and belongs in the none bin, so the bins are shown not to cover everything. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with placeCard, expandCard, revealBin and say. No drag: the agent places a card by naming its bin.
mods.practice: Practice, student operated. The bank from props.questions, one item at a time, each rendering its own cards. Sort a card into its bin, or write the feature that triggered the choice. Scored, with a star finish and a Review phase that walks every item showing the student's placement, the correct bin and the structural note that settles it.
mods.free_play: Free Play, student operated. The student sorts any card, taps a card to see it expanded, and writes their own expression cards to sort. Nothing is scored and nothing is mandatory.

source_tool.name: Identity Match Sort
source_tool.blurb: expression cards sorted into one bin per identity plus a none of these bin that is never empty, so the bins cannot be filled by elimination
source_tool.description: The student matches an expression to the identity that fits its structure, and writes what feature triggered each choice.

theme.premise: A card that looks factorisable turns out not to be, and the class is asked which feature decides
theme.setting: A sorting table with four labelled bins in a row and a spread of expression cards lying face up beneath them
theme.visualStyle: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration
theme.studentPalette: The warmer accent of the same family, with the score and the Finish button carrying it
theme.teacherPalette: The cool indigo accent, low chrome, high contrast, so a projected board stays readable

practice.rating: all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1, never 0
practice.review: The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's placement, the correct bin, and the structural note that explains it.

whatYouLearned: An identity is chosen by reading a structure, not by spotting a squared term
A difference of two squares factorises and a sum of two squares does not
Some expressions match none of the identities, and saying so is a correct answer

text: x squared minus 9 fits an identity. Does x squared plus 9 fit the same one?
scenes.title: ML1 · Easy · Edge Case

buttons.label: Prev
buttons.action: step back one beat; the agent uses the absolute gotoStep

buttons.label: Step k of N
buttons.action: shows position in this mode's sequence, read from walkthrough

scenes.subGoal: The minus sign is the feature that triggers the identity, not the two squares.
scenes.onScreen: The scene built from this checkpoint's own numbers, the question set cleanly above it, and nothing else. One worked item: the cards, the bins, the question, then the correct placements and the structural notes together.
scenes.animation: Card lock: a correct placement settles over 160 ms and the bin count ticks, so the sort accumulates visibly.
scenes.interaction: The agent lands this step with gotoStep, the animation plays, the class predicts out loud, then the agent calls reveal(). The board then fills one line per step.
scenes.valuesShown: Blackboard lines, in order: x squared minus 9 is a difference of two squares, because 9 is 3 times 3. | It factorises as x minus 3 times x plus 3. | x squared plus 9 is a sum of two squares, and no whole number factorisation matches it. | Multiplying x plus 3 by x plus 3 gives x squared plus 6x plus 9, which has a middle term the sum does not. Answer: No: the difference factorises, the sum does not

scenes.subGoal: A perfect square trinomial is recognised by the middle term matching twice the product.
scenes.onScreen: The scene built from this checkpoint's own numbers, the question set cleanly above it, and nothing else. One worked item: the cards, the bins, the question, then the correct placements and the structural notes together.
scenes.animation: Card return: a wrong placement travels back over 220 ms and its structural note writes itself on arrival, so the explanation lands with the card.
scenes.interaction: The agent lands this step with gotoStep, the animation plays, the class predicts out loud, then the agent calls reveal(). The board then fills one line per step.
scenes.valuesShown: Blackboard lines, in order: There are three terms, and the first and last are both squares. | The last term 9 is 3 times 3. | The middle term 6x is 2 times x times 3, which is exactly twice the product of the two roots. | That is the signature of the square of a sum, so it is x plus 3, all squared. Answer: The square of a sum: x plus 3, all squared

scenes.subGoal: The sign of the middle term chooses between the two square identities; the last term stays positive in both.
scenes.onScreen: The scene built from this checkpoint's own numbers, the question set cleanly above it, and nothing else. One worked item: the cards, the bins, the question, then the correct placements and the structural notes together.
scenes.animation: None bin: the first card into the none bin makes the bin brighten once, which marks not fitting as a result rather than a failure.
scenes.interaction: The agent lands this step with gotoStep, the animation plays, the class predicts out loud, then the agent calls reveal(). The board then fills one line per step.
scenes.valuesShown: Blackboard lines, in order: Both have first term x squared and last term 9. | The first has middle term minus 6x, so it is x minus 3, all squared. | The second has middle term plus 6x, so it is x plus 3, all squared. | The last term stays plus in both, because a negative times a negative is positive. Answer: They fit different forms: one is the square of a difference, the other the square of a sum

scenes.onScreen: The scene built from this checkpoint's own numbers, the question set cleanly above it, and nothing else. One worked item: the cards, the bins, the question, then the correct placements and the structural notes together.
scenes.animation: Card lock: a correct placement settles over 160 ms and the bin count ticks, so the sort accumulates visibly.

scenes.valuesShown: Blackboard lines, in order: The identity needs both terms to be squares. | x squared is a square, but 5 is not a square of any whole number. | 2 times 2 is 4. | 3 times 3 is 9, so 5 falls between two squares. | So no whole number factorisation matches, even though the minus sign is there. Answer: Not with whole numbers: 5 is not a square

scenes.onScreen: The scene built from this checkpoint's own numbers, the question set cleanly above it, and nothing else. One worked item: the cards, the bins, the question, then the correct placements and the structural notes together.

scenes.valuesShown: Blackboard lines, in order: Two terms, both squares, joined by a minus, gives the difference of two squares. | Three terms whose first and last are squares, with the middle exactly twice the product of their roots, gives one of the two square identities. | The sign of that middle term then chooses between the sum form and the difference form. | Two terms joined by a plus fits none of them. Answer: The number of terms, whether the outer terms are squares, and the sign of the middle term
